utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. We are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to official reasons. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would like to make a motion to ask the Chamber to reconsider its ruling that was made concerning the mode of testimony of the next witness, Dusan Zurovac. And the reason for that is simply that due to the technical difficulties which we've experienced this week, we have four witnesses still in The Hague to testify over these next two days in which we have shortened work hours, and these people have come -- been here all week and it's very difficult for them to come back. They're working and it's a hardship for them to have stayed here without testifying and also not to -- to be asked to return. So we accept fully that we should not provide the Trial Chamber with more than one revised statement, which we did with Mr. Zurovac and we won't do that ever again; and we also understand that there are materials in paragraphs 2 through 11 in his statement that are not relevant and need not be admitted. But having learned those lessons, without -- we would appreciate it if we could proceed by Rule 92 ter to minimise the time that we would take with this witness's testimony so that the other witnesses can still be heard during the week. And our apologies for our errors in the way we have approached this particular witness's documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. I'm moving over to this end so I can maintain eye contact with the entire Bench. That's why I'm over here. First of all, as a preliminary matter, we don't agree that this is an exceptional circumstance or situation warranting reconsideration. We deal with scheduling issues all the time, for better or worse. This is a matter that we understand involves a relatively short adjustment. We understood from Mr. Robinson the anticipated time for viva voce would be 30 to 45 minutes, in which event the impact is given the amount of time that would normally be taken by or has been consumed by 92 ter submissions and summaries consisting of 10 to 15 minutes, so the impact would be negligible. In any event, this kind of routine and customary scheduling issue is not such that it rises to the level of reconsideration that would upend a Trial Chamber decision. But more importantly, let me get to the issues involved. Mr. Robinson's proposal to eliminate paragraphs 1 through 11 or 2 through 11 really addresses only one part of the issue and clearly the smallest part. The Trial Chamber's principal concern and the one that clearly had the greatest adverse impact on the Prosecution was the steady proliferation of exhibits throughout the course of the week. Now, I emphasise, this comes against the backdrop of hundreds and hundreds of 65 ter violations by the Defence, that is, its failure to provide, pursuant to the Rules, adequate factual summaries of what witnesses were -- what factual issues witnesses were expected to testify to, a matter which left the Prosecution, if it had any hope of attempting to conduct adequate preparation, utterly dependent on the statements. So while under these circumstances the appropriate remedy might well have been to simply preclude any eliciting of the belated information, the Trial Chamber crafted a compromise that would hopefully discourage the Defence from engaging in this practice in the future but allowed it the option and opportunity to elicit such evidence, as was included in that final submission that it saw fit but in the context of a viva voce presentation. Mr. Robinson's proposed solution basically vitiates that compromise. So by eliminating only the material that is admittedly marginal or even meaningless, it allows the accused basically the full benefit of the criticised practice and imposes upon the Prosecution the full burden that the remedy, at least in part, sought to address. So under these circumstances, we consider that there really are only two possible legitimate alternatives. One is maintaining the Court's decision to have all evidence led viva voce. And if the Defence is unhappy with that solution, then the only recourse would be to return to the situation that existed before the addition of the belated information, belated exhibits, and simply lead 92 ter the original statement, that is, paragraphs 1 through 20. Any other proposed solution would be unfounded and unfair. I should note that Ms. West is actually leading the witness. I don't know if she has anything to add that may be of use in this analysis, but other than that, that completes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies for calling up on Mr. Tieger. But, Ms. West, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I don't want to prolong the discussion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having considered the arguments of the parties, the Chamber now gives its ruling. In reaching its oral decision of 12th of November that Dusan Zurovac be led live, the Chamber considered the successive and substantial additions made to the statement proposed for admission as well as the fact that a large portion of the witness's statement covered matters irrelevant to this case. The Chamber is of the view that the arguments put forth by the accused as a basis for reconsideration do not alleviate the Chamber's initial concerns in relation to the witness's evidence being presented pursuant to Rule 92 ter and which led to the Chamber to decide that he be called viva voce. While the Chamber appreciates that witnesses may be inconvenienced by having to travel back to the Tribunal a second time, this is unfortunately a reality of trial proceedings but not one which justifies not hearing a witness live when the Chamber decided that should be the case. The Chamber therefore decides that it will not reconsider its decision that Dusan Zurovac be led live. There's one further issue I'd like to discuss before we continue. Mr. Karadzic, on the 12th of November, 2012, you filed a motion for image distortion for Witness Miladin Trifunovic whose KW number is 515. In paragraph 4 of that motion, the accused states, and I quote: "Dr. Karadzic apologises for the late notice of this requested measure, as Mr. Trifunovic did not raise this issue until he arrived in The Hague." However, the Chamber has been informed by VWS that upon his arrival in The Hague the witness was surprised that protective measures had not been requested, as he had specifically asked for such measures when he met with a member of the Defence team in early to mid-October. So, Mr. Robinson, whether you can provide an explanation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's true that witnesses and our investigators do discuss the possibility of protective measures when they're first contacted. Often much of that took place before the trial started and before the Trial Chamber has denied the protective measures for other witnesses who have similar circumstances. And so we have our Case Manager contacting each witness when we first try to schedule their travel to The Hague and to ask them whether or not they need protective measures so that we could file a motion if they do. And when our Case Manager asked Mr. Trifunovic that, he indicated that he didn't need protective measures so we didn't file a motion for him. And then when he came to The Hague and -- he was disappointed that he didn't have any protective measures. And so we finally discussed it with him and he was willing to nevertheless testify so long as he could at least have image distortion since he was travelling to areas where he felt he could have problems. And so that's why you didn't receive the motion until this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why was he disappointed after having said that he would not need protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't know, Mr. President. I think maybe there was a misunderstanding between him and the Case Manager because he seemed to think that he would have protective measures, but in fact we were informed by the Case Manager, who was talking to witness after witness and has a very strict protocol as to how he's performing those duties, that he hadn't requested any. So I can only think that there was some kind of miscommunication or misunderstanding between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, the Chamber finds it unacceptable that inaccurate representation of the position of witnesses in relation to protective measures find their way into motions before the Chamber. So in the future, the Chamber expect the accused to ensure adequate communication within its team and to ensure that the appropriate attention is given to request -- for protective measures. Witnesses simply cannot be left in the dark until their arrival in The Hague, expecting to be granted protective measures when they have not even been requested. Therefore, it is for the Defence team to adequately inform and advise its witnesses in a timely manner about the request it has or will make in relation to protective measures. Having said that, the Chamber will issue a written decision shortly on that motion. Unless there's any other matters, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just only suggest that this witness have an 90(E) warning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Zurovac, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution, the accused, or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have said to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Excellency. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Zurovac.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'll have to spend a little more time on the examination-in-chief because you will be led viva voce, but I assume that no one has anything against you being provided with your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the exact procedure is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you should know how to conduct your examination-in-chief with the advice of Mr. Robinson and other legal associates. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any problem, Mr. President, with him having his statement? A witness can have a prior statement to assist them whether or not it's admitted under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Tieger -- or Ms. West, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have one observation and that is I believe when that's happened in other Chambers, it's -- the witness has been asked to advise the parties if and when he is referring to the statement so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but we can observe whether the witness consults his statement or not and then we can monitor it. Let it be done. We'll print out the -- do we have B/C/S version? We'll print out the B/C/S version and provide it to the witness. In the meantime, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Zurovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation to be completed. I would like to ask you to do the same. Can you tell us where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of November, 1941, in Nevesinje, in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I'm a professor of literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that what you are by profession? Did you work in your profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo and in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I lived in Novo Sarajevo in Zagorska Street number 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your privately owned house or is it a collective residence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It's my privately owned house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I returned there three months later, about three and a half months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any point in time join the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did you report to the army and could you tell us for what reasons you did this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I reported to the VRS in my neighbourhood, my settlement. It was an exclusively Serbian settlement. I reported there because I didn't want the same thing to happen to me that happened to me in Mostar at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you have in mind? What happened to you in Mostar at the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, 1992, I was imprisoned and I was taken to the central prison in Mostar. On the 18th August I was taken to Stolac and I experienced things that are difficult to understand. It's hard to understand how one man can do such things to another man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which unit did you join? Where was that unit deployed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion deployed in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber where the 4th Company had its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Its area of responsibility was from Pandurevica Kuca and up until the crossroads at Milinkladska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is Ozrenska Street from Zagorska Street, or rather, your house?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, my house is at the corner where Zagorska Street joins Ozrenska Street, to the left, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you assigned some command responsibilities; and if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Not initially, I wasn't assigned any command duties, I was an ordinary private. Later, when the commander of the 4th Company was killed, I became the commander of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was a lieutenant-colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A second lieutenant, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you obtain that rank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: In the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6099.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this map and have you marked it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be scrolled up a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm familiar with this map and I marked this triangle that you can see in the corner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this triangle represent? Is it in blue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in blue. That is the area that was under the control of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this represents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: On the whole, this line is the line of demarcation. That's where the trenches were located and the bunkers on both sides. The enemy was 10, 15, or 20 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, is it necessary to sign the map or can it be admitted as it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he didn't sign -- mark it -- anything on this map in the courtroom, but I need some clarification. Sir, Mr. Zurovac, can you read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who wrote the annotation on this map, Mr. Karadzic? I see "zone of responsibility of D. Zurovac" and further up I see the comment like "no line of sight" and there's "1.250 metres." Who put those markings -- notations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received information from the witness and then we made these notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he also showed where the line should be traced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the blue line is his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you asked only about the blue markings and then the witness said he does not understand or read English. In order for us to admit this as it is, you have to put questions about this comment as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far your area of responsibility is from the area marked as number 10 or 18?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The distance is about a kilometre and a half from number 10 at least, and from number 4, the distance would be about 900 metres, I believe, from the firing position, the distance from the firing position that was under the control of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Were you informed about an incident that took place on the 3rd of September, 1993, in Ivana Krndelja Street?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the Ivana Krndelja Street has been marked here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The Ivana Krndelja Street leaves from -- goes from the bridge over Miljacka up to this hill, there's a vertical line where -- from where incident 4 occurred over the Miljacka river to Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how far is it from your positions to the Ivana Krndelja crossroads and the street that goes from the east to the west?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: About 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a clear line of sight here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between your position and the location marked as number 4; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What, in fact, obstructs this line of sight?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, the lie of the land, the hill is such that you can't see anything from the positions of the 4th Company. You can't see the location where incident 4 occurred. You can see where Tranzit is located here. It was only possible to see this incident, the location of this incident, if you were on the hill behind us. In such a case the distance would be over a kilometre and a half. What is obstructing the line of sight? Well, the hills are obstructing the line of sight. It's a hilly area. We were in some sort of a valley, so there were three or four hills that were obstructing the line of sight. They made it impossible to see the Ivana Krndelja Street. So sometimes the enemy brought through -- brought in manpower and equipment through the Tranzit. We weren't aware of the fact. You can only hear certain sounds that were produced and so on and so forth. You couldn't see anything. I think this thesis is one that doesn't hold water because incident 4 could only have been seen from 400 metres behind our positions, from Gojino hill or Gradon [phoen] hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are those hills in the area of responsibility of the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In such a case, what would the distance be between those points from which you have visibility and location number 4?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: From those points, from Gojino Brdo, the distance would be about 2 kilometres and from Seratlino [phoen] Brdo the distance would be about a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, whether you were informed about the incident that happened on the 22nd of July, 1994, in the Miljenko Cvitkovic Street?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, although I was not the company commander at the time, I had a work obligation at the time. However, there is a lot of illogical things involved in that. It was stated that the boy was standing in front of a shop window. We were behind his back some kilometre and a half away from him and the boy allegedly was hit in the stomach. This doesn't make sense. Let's not even talk about ranges and other things that we will discuss later, whether we could do it or not. There is no either theoretical or practical possibility for us to have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up another document but before that we need the map still. Then I will call up other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, concerning this map we would like to tender it and also I would like to ask that it be added to our 65 ter list. It wasn't on our list because it wasn't in existence at the time we submitted our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I heard evidence regarding number 10 and number 4. I heard 1500 kilometres -- excuse me, metres and 900 metres, but this map has 1.250 metres on it and an extra dot, so if we can have some clarification about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you refer to as extra dots?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't think he said anything about 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not on the map originally?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It may have been, Your Honour, but if this is admitted, it's not going to make any sense otherwise unless he speaks about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not show the witness any documents concerning the location 18. It's a Prosecutor's map and I don't think that this witness knows anything about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I can accept that and perhaps we'll just get rid of that number, but it also regards the 1.250 metres. Unless I'm mistaken, I didn't hear any evidence regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that point, I agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, what's the significance of 1.250 metres on the map?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It's a distance, the distance from our firing positions to incident 10, which is marked on the map. I said about 1500 metres, I said that that was the distance, and that incident number 10 could have been seen only from the hills behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case, that would be even further than your line of defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: About 300 metres. Gojino Brdo is some 350 metres from our positions and Seratino [phoen] Brdo was about 300 metres from our positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the map be admitted? If the witness needs to sign it, I will ask him to sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's okay. You don't have to sign it. We'll admit this. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D6099 receives number D2427.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I just note that the base map is the one that was admitted as P2192, but I note that probably Defence team changed the colour of number 18 from green to yellow, even the legend. I find it amazing. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen I can see number 18 in green --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- both in the captions and when it comes to the figure. They're all green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yellowish-green. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now can we see a photo, this is 65 ter 24026. 24026 pursuant to Rule 65 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this location. I recognise the place, but I could not see it because of the obstructions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, could you repeat your answer so that the interpreters can interpret it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know this area very well because I lived here for almost 30 years; however, the obstructions that are in the Ivana Krndelja Street, I never saw them before, not only me but also none of my soldiers. I can vouch for that with my own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the photo and point to your positions were.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Our positions are in the depth of the photo, about 900 metres from here, but the configuration of the terrain was such that the terrain was sloping. The area is known as Hrasno Brdo or Hrasno hill. It's a hilly terrain, hence the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be assisted in marking Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are the positions visible in this photo, Mr. Zurovac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you draw arrows pointing from the skyline towards the ground to show where your positions were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That would be a problem because as far as I can see, the photo was taken from a position which is somewhere on the road. You can see in the photo that this was not taken from the depth of the terrain where our positions were. This is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I won't ask you to mark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this photo be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, we would like to request that this be added to our 65 ter list, as we didn't contemplate using it until recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And probably the Prosecution may be aware of the provenance of this document, but in the future I would like the accused to introduce where it's from. I can see here it's from Galic trial. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the request is granted and we will admit this into evidence as Exhibit D2428.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My correction. I should have said D2428.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move the photo from the screen, Mr. Zurovac, the road that you see in the photo, was it used by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony I said that the BiH army used this road, but we could not control transit along that road. That's the route of the former railway line. It was a bit below us. There was no visibility. There was no line of visibility from us to there. We could not control that road. They used it to transport manpower and equipment. This street was very busy when it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 24024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, if the accused is going to use many documents which were not listed as -- on the 65 ter list, why don't you deal with in lump sum all together so that we can deal with it more conveniently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be better to do that at the end, perhaps, because I'm not exactly sure how many of these we're going to get to. We're trying to also be conscious of not using too much time. Unless you would like me to make a general request that would apply to any document that he offers during the course of this examination that's not on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution is informed of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they have been included on our Rule 92 ter package, so we are -- they have been informed of them and they have been informed that they were not on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, the Chamber should have been informed of similar documents -- of documents of similar nature. We haven't received any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not following, Mr. President. We filed on the 9th of November our Rule 65 -- Rule 92 ter package which includes the list of documents that were intended to be used with the witness. Now what Dr. Karadzic intends is to select some of those, as time permits, and offer them. So that's what we're working from is our Rule 92 ter package of the 9th of November, and there's a column that indicates which ones were on the 65 ter list and not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all due to various filings, I think. Yes, I found it. Let's proceed. But, Ms. West, do you have any objection in relation to specific documents or you can tell us in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In general, at least the documents I've seen so far, I'm aware of them. I do understand that they're not on the 65 ter list, but they are documents that I've seen. I don't want to make a general -- I don't want to take the general position that the Prosecution does not object to a whole mass load of non-notified 65 ter documents, but in these particular cases these are documents of which I've been aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. On that basis, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this photo depict? What's in the background?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: This is Ivana Krndelja Street, its pavement, and in the background is Hrasno hill, it's the top of Hrasno hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled the summit of Hrasno hill?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That was our area of responsibility. Nobody lived there. There was just an old lady there who had a mentally ill son. People had fled from there so both of those hills, nobody resided there because our line was some 250 or so metres from the tops of any of these hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a line of visibility from the place where this lady is standing and your trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Asimovo Brdo, where was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: If you look at this photo you will see it on the left-hand side, some 900 metres away. Asimovo Brdo is somewhat higher than both Gojino and Seratino Brdo. It's much higher and would be to the left-hand side of the photo as I am looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled Asimovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Asimovo Brdo was dominant together with Gojino and the other hill that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was at least 50 metres higher than the other two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this photo be admitted, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, there have been several questions that have been leading in this matter. I've said nothing. I understand the issue of time, but I don't want Mr. Karadzic to get into the habit of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- as usual practice, I let you go on until objected to. Now you heard Ms. West's submission. Please bear in mind not to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move the exhibit from the screen, can you tell us where the enemy trenches were, looking from this photo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The enemy trenches were below our trenches towards the area where this lady or this man is standing. In other words, enemy trenches would be closer to us. Our trenches were a bit further away. They were some 15 or 20 metres behind their trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Looking at the horizon depicted in the photo, where were the Serb trenches and where were the Muslim trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw a line? Towards the top of the photo you see a white house and then you see a greenish house, and the top of the hill is somewhere there among the houses. And our trenches were below that greenish house. In the photo it would be on my right-hand side. That's where our trenches were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This photo will be admitted as Exhibit D2429.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 65 ter 23968.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph and can you tell us what it shows?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Ivana Krndelja Street. You can see to my left that there are certain skyscrapers, it's Ivana Krndelja Street. All these buildings here, the house that's being built - I don't know whose it is, I don't even know whose house is to the right, the one that has been destroyed. From this position you can't see the location of the incident marked as incident number 4. That's quite simply not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this photograph taken to the north of Ozrenska Street or to the south? Where's Ozrenska Street in relation to this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It's behind this house, behind these trees. It depends because it's not a straight street. It's in a mountainous terrain and the street winds between the houses that were built in the area. It's not to the north -- well, in fact, it's more to the north. Yes, that's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, our positions were here in the depth, in the depth. You can't see where our positions are in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So where was the photographer standing in relation to your positions, was he closer to the Muslims or was he further away from the Muslims in relation to your trenches in fact?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The photograph I was shown a while ago -- well, my impression is that that was taken from Demino hill. They tried to find a good angle to take the photograph, because I'm saying that from the positions of the 4th Company it wasn't possible to see the location of incident number 4. That was, quite simply, impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D2430.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 23967, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you recognise this photograph? What can we see in the photograph and where was the photograph taken from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: You can really see Ivana Krndelja Street in this photograph. It was photographed from the right-hand side. This can be seen because of the layout of the buildings and you can see that these buildings obstructed the line of sight, as well as these residential buildings here, they obstructed the line of sight to incident -- to the location of incident number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which street is Ivana Krndelja Street, the one to the left or the one to the right by these blocks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The skyscraper to the left and the residential buildings are to the right, so it's between the skyscrapers and the residential buildings. That is the location of the Ivana Krndelja Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell where this was taken from, from the ground or from where exactly, from what sort of position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was certainly from some other position, not from the position that was under the control of the 4th Company because it would have been quite impossible to take this photograph from that position. It was to the right, to the town, to Vraca, I mentioned Demino Brdo, Demino hill, a minute ago. Perhaps this photograph was taken from that hill, from Demino hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this photo please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who took these pictures, Mr. Karadzic, by the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, these were taken by the Prosecution and you see the 65 ter numbers are Prosecution 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They were also used in Galic case? Do you know that, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Not at the moment, but I will have that answer for you momentarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this will be admitted as Exhibit D2431.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D6099.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following. Could you tell us whether from your positions in Ozrenska Street, was it possible to use automatic rifles and single shots in order to hit the location marked as number 10 with precision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It would have been impossible to do that. You know that the enemy lines were in front of us and if anyone appeared on a roof and opened fire, for example, on a woman with a child, well, that would have been quite mad. It's a mad idea, a mad assumption. But I'd like to say something else. If you have a look at the previous photograph, if you have a look at the angle or the point from which the photograph was taken, you can see that -- you can see certain things to the right. If you have a look at the location of incident number 4, you can see that the 4th Company is to the left. That's where our area of responsibility is. Why would it be impossible to hit that area? Well, because first of all it's a great distance and an automatic weapon isn't intended to hit targets at such distance. It is possible, but you can't really target such a location. You can't use an automatic weapon because from our positions it was not possible to see the location of incident number 4. That's the first thing. And secondly - and this is incredibly important - do you think people would -- people who were in trenches, who were spending their lives in trenches, do you think they would have the idea of leaving the trenches, climbing up on some sort of hills, and opening fire on some women? Well, that's quite crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would that be crazy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, any honourable man, any honourable combatant, any honourable Serbian combatant wouldn't allow such things. All of these combatants were parents, they had their children, they had their own families. So imagine someone opening fire on a woman and a child, how could such a person know that that woman and that child were Muslims. I'd like someone to explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there also the issue of that person's security if that person climbed up onto a roof?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That would have meant certain death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're gearing towards that direction again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm in a hurry. I'm trying to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have dealt with the incidents. I wanted to ask you about the strength of your company.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, that depended. Its strength depended on the conditions, on the situation in the battle-field. There were 120 men in the company at the most on the basis of the list. However, no more than 80 per cent of them were covering the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were these combatants from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: All these soldiers were on the whole from these private houses. They were quite simply people who were defending their homes and their families. In fact, the families had moved out because it wasn't possible to live there. This might seem to be a sort of fabrication for people who aren't familiar with the situation, but as for the living conditions there, well, that is an entirely different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the age of the men in your unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't favourable and this does demonstrate the fact that people were, in fact, defending their homes, their families. There were quite a few people who, in fact, had never served in the army, so you can't really speak about an elite elected unit. They were there and they had to decide whether to defend themselves or not, whether to live or not. They were just defending their territory, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D20359, 1D20359.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for that to come up, where was the enemy facing you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: At the other end of the line of confrontation. We had a flank line of confrontation. There was the 101st Mountain Unit and then we also had the 102nd Mountain Unit. They were far stronger than we were. The ratio wasn't 10:1, it was 20:1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with this document and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever submit reports to anyone and how frequently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole you submit reports to the battalion commander and this is done twice during the day, about 10.00 in the morning and in the evening, unless there's an extraordinary situation and it's impossible for someone to find time to write anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything about the contents of this document? What is the gist of the document? How is the unit described?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, this document shows that I tried to report to the superior command on the situation in the unit and to report on their age, structure, on the type of men in the unit, because you should bear in mind that these people never had any rest. They didn't leave to have rest. So I informed them about the psychological situation, how well the unit was equipped, and all other negative aspects that involved in the war. This was in 1992. In December we were waiting an attack that was to take place two days later on Gojino Brdo, Gojino hill, and we sustained quite significant casualties there. It was in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20359 receives number D2432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at 23066 -- 1D23060. 1D23060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's noted as one of the associated exhibits. Let us check. I'm told it's not released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic may have read the number wrong. It's 1D20360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about this document.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: This is a report again, a daily report. To tell you the truth, I can't read this, the letters are very small. Could we zoom in a bit so that I can see what it's about? There's just one thing I would like to clarify here. If the men were waiting at the firing position -- well, often we had to ask for assistance because the combatants at the positions were waiting for orders from above. If they did that all the time, they wouldn't survive, because the situation was such that each and every combatant had to take action in order to save his life. So this is a daily report to the battalion command and it shows what the situation was on that day, although I can't see the date at the top of the document. But there's no doubt about the fact that I signed it. It was the 1st of January, new year, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And does it say -- well, that was for yesterday, but does it say that today the enemy hasn't opened fire nor have you and you don't have water?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: We don't have water, we don't have electricity, we have nothing. The conditions can't be described. The people who are listening to this now can't even understand what the situation was like. It's impossible to understand what people are prepared to do in order to defend their honour, to defend their lives, and to defend their homes, and so on and so forth, to defend their icons and their religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2433.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the course of the examination we would actually like to tender a number of reports similar to this that has been shown to the witness in the proofing process that describe the daily life on the line where he was working and are authored by him. And I was wondering whether or not the Chamber would allow Dr. Karadzic to simply elicit from the witness that he has had the opportunity to review the specified documents which are in the statement and that they appear to be reports authored by him which describe the situation at his position during the war. And if that would be sufficient, we could save a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would object to this procedure. It was something that I think we discussed even with a witness that I took during the last portion of the Prosecution case in chief. We did it through a 92 ter process, where a lot more information was elicited about a list of documents that she had put together. It was at that point that Mr. Robinson objected and I make the same objection here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further -- if my memory serves correct, it's not consistent with the Chamber's past practice. If they're relevant, put them to the witness; otherwise, there's no need for those documents -- I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is of the view that if Mr. Karadzic wants to tender those documents, he needs to put those documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has this been admitted? Yes. I'd like to call up 1D20361. 1D20361.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, can you tell us briefly, is this your document? When was it drafted and what does it represent in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't see much. In any case, it was around Christmas 1993. It's not very visible. It says here yesterday around 12.00, or rather, 12.20, the enemy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is impossible to interpret because the witness is reading too fast and mumbling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, the interpreters are not able to keep up with your speed, so could you slow down when reading out something. So could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report, a daily report, sent to the battalion command which was drafted on the 7th of January, 1993, on Orthodox Christmas. One can see from this report that on Orthodox Christmas, the enemy launched an attack on our positions from the line on the flank, from Asimovo Brdo, which was the biggest threat for us in any case. In this report I mention some of the shortcomings and shortages. There were a lot of such things, both in our lives as well as in war time, especially in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Combined artillery and infantry attack." What is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: First there is artillery support to move us from our trenches, and after that the infantry starts using grenades and infantry weapons in order to move our line in their favour. I suppose that they counted with the fact that it was a holiday, that the men had gone home to celebrate, and they thought that our strength was diminished and that's why they attacked us, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here that there was indiscriminate shelling. What kinds of shells were used against you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Interestingly enough, when it comes to shelling in this specific case and in general, that company was like a gateway for all those who wanted to break through our firing positions, to break us up, to open Sarajevo, but it's not a good word because Sarajevo was enclosed. That's why I'm not using the word "to open" Sarajevo. However, they wanted to break us up and to move us further in the depth of our positions and that would have given them the control of entire Ozrenska Street. That was the main goal. It is very important for those who know the situation in the case that they had broken up our lines, they would have come behind our lines and they would have captured the entire unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the last sentence to see what that is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Scroll up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this out aloud.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Of course I can. "How do we regulate the men's rest? I'm afraid that exhaustion and tiredness will take their toll." Let me explain, those people were on the front line from the first day to the last day without any breaks. People who had a bath only exceptionally, perhaps once in a month or even in two months. The conditions of life were such that a normal mind cannot grasp that, as I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? I'm looking at the time. I'm in your hands about the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be admitted as next exhibit, i.e., Exhibit D2434, and we'll break for 25 minutes and resume at 13 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can interrupt. Just one quick administrative matter. There were two photos that were used during the direct and you had asked the provenance of them. Both were used in the Galic case, that's D2428 and D2429. In the first one, 28, that's the photo we saw that vantage point was the street and we saw a bunch of hash -- or lines on it and that was used in the Galic case with the victim of the sniping incident, Nafa Taric, and she was drawing the barricades. As for D2429, again that was a photo actually of Nafa Taric of the location of the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about 2430 and 2431?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do not believe those were used in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But they are from the Prosecution. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D20346.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, please, in a nutshell, tell us what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I can't see the document well, I can't read it, because the letters are too small. I can answer your question. I know what this document is about. It speaks about very bad conditions in the unit. In addition to the age, structure, in addition to absenteeism from the defence line, there were other problems in the unit. People leave without permission and I informed the commander that the situation in the unit is alarming. This is a daily report for the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who cosigned the report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It was Ljubo Bozic who was actually the driver of the unit's lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20346 receives number D2435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D20351.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, what does this document contain? It was issued on the 12th December 1993.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Can this be zoomed in? I'll try to read it. This was -- this is the situation as I found it. I can say that we never provoked the enemy during a cease-fire. We were never in a situation to provoke them because the enemy was much more powerful and it actually suited us when there was a cease-fire, when there was no shooting, because we knew that the enemy was much stronger than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the UNPROFOR visit that is mentioned here, can you tell us how often UNPROFOR visited you, whether they found it difficult or easy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR came very often to our line because it was one of the most difficult lines on the Sarajevo front line. I suppose that an agreement would be reached not to open fire. I don't know how objective their reports were. I hope that they were. They would come and they would see the same things that I mentioned in my daily reports. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, here you say that soldiers were forced to fire back. Could you explain to us how or why were those soldiers forced to fire back in response to the provocation from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is self-evident. If they opened artillery fire in support of a future infantry attack, people who were in trenches would respond. To avoid a situation where they would be captured alive they had to return fire in order to save their lives because the enemy was only 15 or 20 metres away from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My question is this: You referred to enemy fire as provocation. What would have happened if you had not fired back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case we would either have to withdraw or we would have all been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would not have been provocation. What did you mean here by "provocation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Provocation, those were short bursts of fire on our positions along the entire separation line. Sometimes those provocations ended without any further, more complex actions. That would be provocation. That was done to disturb peace in the unit. People could not feel safe and at ease. All means were used in order to put us in an unfavourable position. That's how things are done in war time. I would call this a type of special warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be admitted as Exhibit D2436.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have to correct the transcript. The witness said that that fire could be preparation for an imminent attack, not a future attack as an attack sometime in the future. The witness used the word "imminent," not "future," and that's why there was response to the fire. A future attack can happen any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that you used the word "imminent," Mr. Zurovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. That was some sort of announcement. The enemy could have given up on that. However, it could have been an introduction into an attack or aggression against our line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D20354. Can this be zoomed in for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a similar report. Can you explain its meaning, especially here where you say that provocations were stepped up during the night along the entire line of defence. "At 3.00 we had to respond and shut the enemy down."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: We suffered most problems from the 101st Mountain Brigade which was on our right-hand side flank. If we were provoked by the unit that was in front of us towards the Ivana Krndelja Street, the unit on our flank opened mortar fire and fire from all other types of weapons. We suffered major losses as a result of that. In my company I lost 54 men, not even including those men that had come to assist us and civilians. It was a killing field, a true execution site. Maybe I should continue. We didn't have electricity, we didn't have water. To be even more specific, sometimes we did not even receive food for a fortnight. It was very risky for anybody to come to us, to our unit, because on two occasions the drivers that were bringing us food were killed in their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we can see that you had some people who had defected. How often did that happen? What was their ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It happened very often. They were Serbs. They would take opportunities when they were in trenches together. They usually paid those who were with them. They would put a sign on their chest on which it says: Don't shoot, I'm a Serb. There were a lot of such instances, especially when Croats and Muslims started fighting. On that day as many as 24 men crossed over to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that they were Serbs. Were they Serbs or mostly Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Serbs. When I say 24 men, I mean when the Muslims and Croats started fighting, those were mostly Croats who defected on that day. The rest of them were exclusively Serbs. Let me explain. They had been members of the BH army before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's Corkovic's name, in fact, is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Where is that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second line, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Corkovic, Serb, and the other person who was a policeman was sent the psychiatric hospital. People fought in such situations. They'd lose it, they'd spatially and temporally lost. People would simply lose it. They wouldn't know where they were, they wouldn't realise that they were in danger. So I don't know what this person's ethnicity is. I stated that he was allegedly a policeman here, Hibor [phoen] Corkovic, but he was sent to Sokolac to the mental ward for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Figuric, that is a Croatian surname. Was this person a Croat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That's quite possible. I can't remember exactly because a lot of years have passed since then --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think this is of huge consequence, but I just again want to remind Mr. Karadzic of the form of his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20354 receives number D2437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D20352.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this document. What does it say in the first line? I'll read it out. It says: "On the basis of observations, the enemy is massing forces in Zagorska Street ..." Is that your street?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I have to clarify this. When I mentioned the byroad a while ago, we don't actually see it. At the foot of Zagorska Street, it was possible for them to bring in lorries to transport two batteries, for example, that we couldn't even see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't open fire on them, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, we didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's -- I don't know if he doesn't understand or he's not listening --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you fire on them when they brought in manpower and equipment to that area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, because we couldn't see anything and we couldn't just open fire blindly for numerous reasons. First of all, we couldn't see the enemy; and secondly, we would be using a lot of ammunition and this doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to these attacks and provocations, with regard to the fire that was opened on your area of responsibility in Ozrenska Street, what was your opinion of this, what was your attitude toward this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, as I said a while ago, I said what was at stake. It was quite simply a matter of clearing that area of Serbs in Sarajevo. They were to be driven out towards Lukavica and later this was, in fact, done in accordance with the Dayton Agreement. These people were, quite simply, driven away and Sarajevo now is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not admit this? This is a different one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20352 receives number D2438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D20356. Could we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the first two sentences. Could you please tell us something about them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: "Yesterday at 1145 hours the enemy improvised an attack on our lines or on the lines of the 2nd and 3rd Platoon. The attack lasted for 20 minutes. We were forced to return fire. There were no consequences for our combatants. Yesterday we visited the lines ..." and so on and so forth. So this is a quite usual war of attrition. There are such customary provocations. In the course of the day and in the course of the night, a unit is provoked. As I said a while ago, it's a special type of war, you try to exhaust the combatants. If the combatants can have a rest and sleep -- if they can't sleep and rest, well, the enemy is constantly opening fire because they're rested, more rested than we are, and this is, in fact, why they engage in such provocations, in order to incapacitate the other side, the unit, my unit, in fact, if I can put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20356 receives number D2439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D20362, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just ask when the document is brought up if I can at least briefly see the English. I'm familiar with these documents, but I just want to see it for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not possible to follow in English with your personal computer?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I was only seeing the B/C/S for the last few documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's probably --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Oh -- yes, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because the witness said he was not able to see the small fonts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I understand, and I realise why you're doing it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- but if we could just -- and I can manage it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would also appreciate it if we could see the English on the screen as it is difficult to follow when the witnesses read at such speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the first sentence and what does it mean, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: "For several days, from 1400 to 1500 hours, the enemy has been shelling our positions with 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortars. About a dozen shells fell yesterday of an unknown calibre. There were no casualties. Material damage was huge ..." Well, what I have to say is in the course of the war, shells that aren't customary did appear and professional soldiers and officers didn't know where they had been made, where they had come from. In such cases, you have artillery preparations which is followed by an infantry attack, et cetera. So if you have a look at the document, the one from yesterday and all these reports, you can see that attempts are constantly being made to move our positions behind the Mojmilo hill, towards Lukavica -- or, in other words, attempts are being made to drive people away from our territory, our houses, our ancestral land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why is the material damage huge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, one of their batteries was behind the railway station and sometimes heavy artillery would completely destroy a privately owned house. It would raze the house to the ground. These weren't isolated events. There's probably a document about this and photographs that show that this happened. An entire house might be destroyed by artillery fire and not only one house. For example, if they thought that our people were in those houses, the houses would be covered by fire and only the foundations, the concrete foundations, of those houses would remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20362 receives number D2440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D20367.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the first and last sentences.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: "Recently, enemy snipers have been particularly active, beginning to shoot at around 0700 hours and going on throughout the day." That's a fact. "Yesterday in Gojino Brdo, Mihajlo Brbonjic was lightly wounded, but was sent back to his position having been treated at the clinic. "This morning the enemy sniper was active again. Troop movements have been reduced to a minimum."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be useful to point out that the snipers opened fire from the skyscrapers at Pero Kosoric Street. They were at the level of our lines so they could cover our lines. They could completely cover our lines. Whenever someone appeared -- well, the troops would joke, they'd put someone's cap on a pole, raise it, and then they would open fire. Fabrika -- the factory Zrak remained in Sarajevo, they produced sights there, so they had a lot of snipers. They had these snipers, that's one thing. And secondly, all those who were involved in shooting before the war as a sport were engaged as snipers. So not only in our units but in all units snipers inflicted quite a lot of harm.
