utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I fear that in line 10 something missed. The witness said that there were men who had been -- who practiced shooting as a sport before the war and they were engaged by the enemy. Is that what you said, Mr. Zurovac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just say whether there were any civilian casualties as a result of this sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In Ozrenska Street, as I said, a hundred men from my company were killed. They're men who came to assist us, men from my unit as well. In the area under our control, over 20 civilians were killed. There were seven or eight women who were killed. What did the snipers do? Well, it's very sad, but they targeted everything. In the area of Vraca they killed a cow. So they would fire on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D20367 becomes Exhibit D2441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, which unit was facing you, which Muslim unit was facing you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I've already said that there was the 101st Mountain Brigade on our flank and below us there was the 102nd Motorised and Infantry and Mountain Brigade. The 101st and the 102nd Brigade. One was facing us and the other was on our flank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of weapons did your enemies have? As far as you know, what sort of fire did you come under?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning until I appeared there, I think that we had better weapons, but soon, once I had arrived, they had all types of weapons. And later when I left, I think that their weapons were even better than ours. So they had all types of weapons that are used in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could have some understanding for this document. Could it be admitted into evidence. I would just like the witness to see 1D02681, 1D02681.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that area of responsibility, was there a change in units? Were there any changes apart from the names of the units or did they remain as they were throughout the war-time period?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: They remained as they were. As far as I know, our units remained as they were. The beginning -- perhaps there was some changes, but nothing much. Perhaps the unit would be given a different code, the men remained where they were from 1992 up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at this order from the 101st Brigade and tell us what sort of artillery they had and where did the commander of the 101st Brigade deploy these weapons, and does this tally with the information you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Could this please be enlarged because it's really not very legible. If we could enlarge it, that would be good because I can't read it at all. I see that 120-millimetre weapons are mentioned, 105-millimetres, 82-millimetres, and so on and so forth. We knew about that. Well, how did we know about that? Because of the action they took. From August 1993 until the end of the war they had superior fire-power, not only superior manpower. Here you can see that they had all types of weapons and we know this for two reasons. We know this because when they would open fire on us, we knew what they were using. Soldiers know what is being used to open fire, and there were quite a few Serbs who defected from their units. They came over to our side. And these people provided us with information on the weapons that they had and on the lines that they were holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now ask you to have a look at the part that says "VP" and tell us what that means. Do you know anything about these locations that were facing your line, the line of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know these locations. You should bear in mind the following. A minute ago, I said that Asim hill and Milina Kosa -- when you go towards Milinkladska Street, well, in that area they can dominate our positions. This is important to bear in mind. And secondly, as you are probably aware, they often opened fire from all buildings, all roofs. You can see this in the documents. In a letter from General Morillon, Izetbegovic and his artillery located at the hospital in Kosevo -- he is warned about that and they opened fire from all those locations. And they would put a lot of mortars on lorries so these mortars would be mobile. And they would fire a few shells for -- and then they would change their location. So in such cases there was nothing we could do. We didn't have such possibilities. As I said a while ago, the byroad below Hrasno -- no units from our company could control that byroad. Anything could happen there and we wouldn't be aware of it because we couldn't observe anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless it's a leading question, I hope I can put this. Do you know these who have 82 mortars, three of them, were they positioned in an inhabited area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second firing position in the annex?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, the same thing applies. You see, normally people are mistaken in what they believe these fire -- firing positions to be or targets because normally they would target inhabited areas, hospitals, et cetera. From the military point of view, they were legitimate military targets. However, then the question would arise of them having shelled an inhabited area. Those who were on the spot were able to see that this wasn't true because with very few exceptions, Sarajevo was the say it was, bearing in mind the separation lines that didn't see that much fighting. After all, Mr. Ghali said himself when he visited Sarajevo that there were places that had seen far worse fighting than was the case there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With some flexibility toward the Defence, can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D02681 becomes Exhibit D2442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that. Thank you to Mr. Zurovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One other question. Mr. Zurovac, you're a writer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am done with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just have a moment, please. May I ask for the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to take up on one of the documents that Mr. Karadzic showed you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have D2434, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is one of your documents from January 7th, 1994. And in his question to you at page 33, line 21, today, he said: "You say here there was indiscriminate shelling ..." And you went on to answer that question affirmatively. Can you tell us, looking at this document, to what part of it you referred when you spoke about "indiscriminate shelling"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Let me just see, let me find that. Can you point me to the paragraph where I said that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, that's my question for you. I want you to point me to the paragraph where it talks about indiscriminate shelling.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't understand you. You want me to ask you where indiscriminate shelling took place? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, let's try this again. When Mr. Karadzic showed you this document he said that this document suggests that there was indiscriminate shelling of your positions or of -- out of the city onto Bosnian Serb areas. Show me in this document where it says there was indiscriminate shelling.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't see that place here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move on. You spoke earlier today --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I draw the attention of everybody in the courtroom to line 5, which starts with the words "around 1400 hours the enemy shelled our positions randomly or indiscriminately and at irregular intervals ..." I don't know whether this has been interpreted or not, but here in the Serbian it says clearly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At around 1400 hours the enemy shelled our positions randomly and at irregular intervals. About 10 times 82-millimetre shells fell ..." That's correct. Your question was what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I find it inappropriate for you to intervene for that reason. You can take up that issue in your re-examination. But, Ms. West, would you like to take up from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In this sentence: "The enemy shelled our positions randomly ..." When you say "our positions," you mean your military positions, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Shells can fall short or overreach. So this is random shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Of your positions, so the "positions" means military positions, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier today you spoke about -- at transcript page 34 you said that the enemy: "... wanted to break through our firing positions, to break us up, open Sarajevo, but it's not a good word because Sarajevo was enclosed. That's why I'm not using the word 'open' ..." Can you tell us now exactly what do you mean? Is it your position that Sarajevo was encircled?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That was not my position. Sarajevo is closed from the inside. In Sarajevo there were criminals who became high-ranking officers in the enemy army overnight. There is a sea of documentation about women who asked the mayor who was in Dobrinja when Sarajevo would be open and he said Sarajevo would be open when the last German mark leaves the pockets of the poor people and ends up in the hands of the criminals. If we are talking about the encirclements, we can talk about three different circles around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness should be kindly asked to speak slower. It is impossible to interpret every word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, in order for the Chamber and the public to understand what you are saying through interpreters, please slow down when you speak. Please speak slowly. Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard from several witnesses already and there are more to come who indicate that there was an SRK policy of containment of Sarajevo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it was the objective of the 2nd Battalion to keep the city under siege, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Court will hear some evidence from another Defence witness that that was exactly the case, that the 2nd Battalion was purposely put there to keep the city under siege. Your disagreement with this notion, can you tell us the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think when putting that proposition to the witness and for the parties, we should at least hear who is being referred to, if necessary in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, who is Milan Hrvacevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Milan Hrvacevic was an assistant battalion commander. I can explain why Milan Hrvacevic spoke the way he did. Milan Hrvacevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, thank you. Let me ask you this: He was the deputy commander of the 2nd Battalion, correct? Your battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not allowed to interrupt Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he didn't answer the question put by Ms. West so she was directing to answer her question, but let us see. Let's continue. We'll allow the witness to answer any questions and we'll not stop the witness. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, he was the deputy commander of your battalion; correct ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as you've already indicated, you understand that he said that the 2nd Battalion was there to keep the city under siege. So my question for you is: Since Mr. Hrvacevic was higher up in command than you, do you think he might have had more information than you to make such a statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: When was this statement provided and under what conditions? Maybe that would be interesting. It is well-known that Milan Hrvacevic went there to interpret at UNPROFOR. He was captured. He was beaten up. He was tried, and subsequently it turned out that all those statements were not valid, they were all refuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, that didn't answer my question. But would he -- let's try it again. Would he have been in a position to have more information than you, such that he would have made this statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, may we know to whom this statement was made, was it made to the OTP or to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, fair enough. It was an OTP statement in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now the English translation has been completed. Could you repeat your question, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would Milan Hrvacevic have been in a position to have more information than you such that he would have made this statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's calling for speculation as to what motivation he might have had to make that statement. If she wants to ask him what was his position and what was the witness's position, then that's one thing; but to speculate as to why he would have made that statement, we don't think that the witness is capable of giving an answer to that question that's helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we move on, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke today about several documents and in a few of them we saw that you employed the term "provocation" when describing ABiH fire coming out of the city. And the Honourable Judge Kwon asked you specifically what you meant by that term. And one of the things you said in response is: "It could have been an introduction into an attack or aggression against our line." Sir, would you agree with me that the term "provocation," was, in fact, an effort to break the siege -- or what you term "provocation" to be was, in fact, an effort to break the siege?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Absolutely, I stand behind my words.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So just to be clear, when you say they were provoking the SRK, you believe that they were trying to break the siege?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Not only do I believe that; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you think they were justified in trying to break the siege?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I suppose it was justified from the point of view of an intention to take the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to place it under control, and to create a state that would suit the policy of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that shortly. But tell us, do you think that one of the reasons they were trying to break the siege was lack of food and supplies that they had within the city?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't think so. You know only too well that Sarajevo had a tunnel under the airport and that through that tunnel they transported not only food and footwear and clothes, but even weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24069A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a report from the UNHCR office, the Special Envoy for the former Yugoslavia. It's the entire report -- it's a compilation of reports, but we are going to look at specifically one that's dated June 1993. This is a period of time when you were there. And on the right-hand corner, "One year of air-lift" -- and I believe there should be B/C/S, but I'll go slowly through this. "One year of the air-lift" on the right-hand side, it talks about: "... Sarajevo air-lift celebrating its 4.000th flight to the besieged capital, having flown 44 million kilos of humanitarian relief items. The air-lift started on July 3rd, 1992, and some 20 nations have contributed ..." It goes on in the middle of the paragraph. "After over one year of siege, Sarajevo survives thanks to the resilience of the population and the aid ..." And then the next paragraph, there's a comment from the High Commissioner, and she said: "... 'condemns the actions of those who are blocking the delivery of food, medicine, fuel, water, power, gas, and other humanitarian assistance in a cowardly attempt to starve and kill innocent civilians.'" Now, sir, do you not agree with me that one of the reasons the ABiH would want to break the siege is because they were lacking in all these things that she just mentioned, food, medicine, fuel?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, not fully. In Sarajevo people who were starving were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. It was a state of war. You cannot look at things so narrow mindedly. If Sarajevo was the biggest camp in Europe, it would be a camp for the Serbs. I don't agree with this because we were never in a situation to stop a humanitarian convoy or do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document and it's not directly contradictory to his testimony in the sense that it's not something he would be expected to have known about in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was June 1993. This man had already been there for almost a year and on -- right on the outskirts of this sieged area. Although he's suggesting that other people were suffering as well, it directly goes to impeachment of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees that this document is related to the credibility of the witness, so for that reason, only for that reason, we'll admit this. So we'll admit this to the extent it relates to the -- relates to this witness's -- relates to the impeachment of this witness's evidence. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Would that be limited to the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24069A receives number P5988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let me put a theory to you and then I'm going to ask you a question about it. It has been your suggestion and generally the Defence case that the ABiH attacks or provocations, as you put it, were offensive in nature and that the SRK only responded. Yet, by virtue of the siege, the entire event was offensive in nature on the part of the SRK because it was the encircling party. To keep the city under siege and perhaps even to split the city required offensive measures by the SRK. And by "offensive," I mean aggression and I mean what you term as "provocation." And in this case, the ABiH was trying to deblock the city to get the city open. Do you disagree with my position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't disagree -- I don't agree with it. How can a person be an aggressor against his own country, against his own house? This is what I'm wondering. Is that possible? Can 15.000 people hold a siege around the 60.000 men in the 1st Sarajevo Corps? These are my counter questions in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, I can understand -- I gather what your position is, but I would ask you to not ask any questions and just try to respond so we can get through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 240 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, I note the time. It's time to take a break. We'll break for 25 minutes. And I see that the -- whether the nature of the attack, offensive or defensive, was raised by the Defence in the first place, but I was wondering whether we are not gearing towards the realm of jus ad bellum. So please bear that in mind. We'll take a break and resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have 65 ter 24078, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated December 16th, 1993, and under the first paragraph -- can you see this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I can't read anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I can agree it doesn't look great, but I will go slowly through it. Paragraph 1 says: "The enemy did not give up from their offensive intentions to unblock Sarajevo and link the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Corps of the so-called ABiH on the line ..." and it names some places "aiming to split our forces and bring them into an unfavourable operational position."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Under "the commander's decision" it says: "I decided to perform an active defence with the Corps' main forces ..." Let's just stop there for a moment. Sir, can you tell us what active defence means?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: That means that the units were in a state of readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Doesn't that just mean -- isn't that just another term for offence, active defence is the same as offence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No. The idea of defence doesn't contain with -- doesn't contain the idea of offence, of offensive action.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go down. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to comment on the transcript. It says that defence excludes the idea. It doesn't say it does not contain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much difference and the interpreters noted that there's no difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we continue on, at the end of this paragraph it talks about the goals and it says: "... the main goal to: "Prevent the Muslim forces from unblocking their part of the town and the occupation of the special purpose industrial objects ..." Sir, do you agree with me that what the Muslims were trying to do, the ABiH forces, was trying to break the siege?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to in English page 5. It's page 3 of the B/C/S. I think we're there on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Under (b), this still regards goals, it says: "In the area of Sarajevo take control over ..." and it lists a number of places "and later on, upon the arrival of fresh forces, take control over Mojmilo, by executing operational activities from Hrasnica cut the communication towards Igman and Central Bosnia to Muslims from Sarajevo; link the operational formation of the Corps in the Lukavica - Ilidza axis and establish conditions for the division of Sarajevo in two parts." Sir, would you agree with me that splitting Sarajevo into two would constitute an offensive act by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent, yes. But I would like to know when this order was issued. I would like to know what the date of the order is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document dated December 16th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24078 receives number P5989, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P05980. This is a document the Trial Chamber saw very recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is dated April of 1994. Thank you. And under "tasks" it says Muslim forces -- under 2. "Muslim forces are creating conditions for unblocking Sarajevo and launching attacks along other axes and lines of contact with our units." If we go to number 8, which is the next page of the English, it says: "Fortify positions around Sarajevo by erecting wire and concrete barriers which would in turn strengthen the belief that they are really blocked ('in a camp')." Now, sir, by April of 1994 you had been there already for some time, at least November of 1992. Had you seen any wire or concrete barriers around the city like described in this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, no, I really hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, today at page 47 you were talking about weapons and you were making a comparison between the weapons the SRK had and the ABiH had, and you said: At the beginning until I appeared there I think we had better weapons but soon they had all types of weapons. And then you looked at a document that was dated June 13th, 1995, it was an ABiH document, and you made some comments on it. I'd like to talk a little bit more about the comparison of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the first thing I'd like to look at is 65 ter 07737. It's a map -- and, Mr. President, I know the witness is having difficulties seeing this. I wonder if the usher could actually give him the map itself. It might be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Again, this is -- it's map 30 in the Sarajevo map book.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is the map that you have on the screen in front of you. And you can -- can you tell us what the title of this map is? What does it say in the middle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Commander's decision with regard to the attack Lukavica 95 -- well, we had a work obligation at the time, I have to point this out, so I'm not familiar with this at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. But I want to talk about 1995 in regards to weapons because during your direct you already spoke about the month of June 1995 and regarding weapons. I want to look at the little white box in the bottom of this map and you can turn the page of your book and you will see it bigger.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't read anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you turn the page of that map book, you will see it in very large print. There you go. So this is an SRK balance of forces in 1995, and on the left-hand side we see SRK forces and their equipment and on the right-hand side we see ABiH forces and their equipment. And if you look through this you'll see that the SRK had four tanks, ABiH had two; SRK had four 155 howitzers, ABiH had one; SRK eight 122 howitzers, ABiH five. And as you go through it, you'll then see SRK had 14, 105 howitzers, ABiH two. And then we'll go down to mortars, they had 36 to 18, 120-millimetre mortars, ABiH had 12; SRK had 40, 82-millimetre mortars, ABiH had 16. Sir, contrary to your position earlier today, would you agree with me by the SRK's estimation, it had far more weapons than the ABiH did in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, I was speaking about infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So your limit your earlier testimony to infantry weapons and not these types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: As regards 120-millimetre mortars, did your battalion have 120-millimetre mortars while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't know about the battalion, but I do know that my company did not have any such mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about 82-millimetre mortars, did your battalion have those?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about multiple-rocket launchers, did the battalion have those?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have -- may I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the witness hasn't confirmed anything from that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because it's related to his evidence he gave in examination-in-chief and also credibility, we'll admit this. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07737 becomes Exhibit P5990, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P5984, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the 65 ter number 7737 also include the zoomed legend? If it does not, let's include it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we're going to look at a document from June of 1993. This regards your 2nd Battalion and your company, and this is a period of time when you were in the company; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this an accurate representation of what -- the status of ammunition in your company at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember now whether this is correct, whether this was actually the status, but I assume that to be the case, although this was signed by the commander who preceded me. He was killed. But I assume that this was the situation. I was present there at the time but in the capacity of a private.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And number 7 and 8, grenades 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre, those refer to mortar shells; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P5983, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this moves into October of that same year, so a little bit later. It's a list of weapons in your company, and again it's signed by the previous commander to you. But do you have any reason to believe that this is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: It's not accurate because it was signed by a driver of the lorry. I have to clarify certain things here. Since a mortar detachment was formed earlier on far from our rear, then when we believed there might be an attack, we would report to the battalion command and they would send us two or three mortars. Because if you know what a mortar is and what mortar fire is, well, if you have 50 metres between the lines, then you can't use the weapon because the shell might hit the person who fired it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's exactly right and the Trial Chamber has heard evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move to P5985, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is actually a document signed by you and it's December of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as regards these -- this ammunition you wrote: "We have none of the above-mentioned ammunition. I request that you deliver this ammunition to me." And included in this are 60-millimetre mortar shells and 82-millimetre mortar shells. So you agree by December 1993 you had been using those type of mortar shells, had you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I apologise, was this 1993 or 1995. It's not very legible. If it's 1993, I'll go back to what I was saying. If it's December 1993, we were expecting an attack that took place in December, in fact, and we asked the battalion command to supply us, to provide us, with two mortars and with ammunition that we did not have in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But just two months earlier there is a list of weapons for the company in which it was listed 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars, suggesting that you did have those types of mortars two months earlier; and then six months earlier it was the same indication. So are you suggesting now that prior to December of 1993 you did not have mortars?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, I'm not trying to say that. I don't know what the situation was before I came to the unit and before I became company commander. Every company had mortars, but when the mortar platoon was established in the rear on a hill -- well, this isn't the front lines for good reasons because that would be in the vicinity of the enemy. So when that mortar platoon was established on Poljino [phoen] hill, when we had information according to which an attack might be launched, we report to the battalion command. The battalion command would take two or three mortars and they were given to us as assistance in such cases. In December, a few days after that event, there was an intense attack on Gojino hill. We lost some of our positions and we sustained quite significant casualties. This was on Gojino hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us what type of targets you would use 60- and 82-millimetre mortars for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: We could only fire on the flank. We couldn't fire in front of us. It was on the flank where the enemy was located and where our unit was located. That was behind Asimovo hill. There used to be a prison there and their units were deployed there and they threatened us from the flank. So we could only fire on the flank with these shells. In front of our line, it would have been interesting if someone had been harmed by mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to repeat the last sentence, which was not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zurovac, could you kindly repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it would be interesting if we could determine the situation at the front line. As far as I know, there were no casualties towards Dolac Malta, that's the front line, no one died as a result of mortar shells. This is at least the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, as I understand your testimony, you only used the mortars to fire behind you and not in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: What do you mean behind us? You're not right. I'm talking about our flank. I don't know how your people are interpreting. I'm talking about our flank. The deployment of the company towards Mol [phoen]. There is a flank, that's what I mentioned a little while ago where there was the 1st Mountain Company and the area which was our forward position towards Malta.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Transcript, two interventions. First of all, on line 4, page 69, the witness said: Such weapons are not kept on the forward line. Second of all, here the flank is being interpreted as "behind" instead of "beside." The witness never said "behind," it should have been interpreted as "beside," instead it was interpreted as a "flank."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Apart from that issue of flank, could you repeat your intervention with respect to page 69.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the witness stated that when that battery or that group was established, the mortars were moved behind the lines because such weapons are not kept on the forward line. And this was not recorded when the witness stated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript says -- reflects that -- as witness -- witness as having said: "But when the mortar platoon was established in the rear on a hill -- well, this isn't the front line for good reasons because that would be in the vicinity of the enemy." I think that reflects what you suggested, Mr. Karadzic. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it would be really good if the interpretation was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, it's with that speed interpreters are having very hard time -- to keep up with us. Yes, let's continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so that I clearly understand, it's your testimony that you never used mortars to fire in depth into the city of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now today at the beginning of your testimony you spoke about a number of -- or at least two of the sniping scheduled incidents and you were giving us some ranges. Now, just so that we are absolutely clear, your company covered part of Ozrenska Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it not true that there were at least 12 snipers in the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, I really wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were there any in your company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24077, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a document, part of which is handwritten, and it's from January 1994, signed by you. Now the part that we see is handwritten, do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: This is the handwriting of a foot soldier, but it's neither here nor there. You can ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. This appears to be a listing put together of fugitive soldiers or soldiers who deserted. I'd like to go to number 25 in the list, and under number 25 we have Rajko Ciro - excuse my pronunciation - and it says here "AP," the registration number, and then "sniper." Under that "automatic M56 sniper" and then there's a word in your language. Tell me what this represents. What does that information represent to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: This list was compiled of those men who had left the unit with weapons. This person, Ciro Rajko, who unfortunately got killed, he left. For a while he was an assistant company commander. He left and he took this sniper rifle with him. I don't know how he had gotten by it. The weapons had been obtained much before I joined. While I was there, I'm sure that we did not have a single sniper rifle in the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene on the transcript once again. A very important word is missing from the transcript. The witness said: This is a list of the men who had left the unit with weapons and they were being searched for the weapons that they had taken with them. That's why they were being searched, and this was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is actually a list of the weapons who had been taken by people. One went to Nevesinje and the other to Visegrad, and this is a list of weaponry that had been taken by the people who left the unit and we were looking for those weapons. And those people had been issued with those weapons in 1992. We were looking for them and this is a list of the weapons and the people that we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Lattanzi also confirms that it was so translated into -- in French. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This document is dated December 1994. So by this time you had been in this company for well over a year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you said that this particular person left the unit with a sniper rifle but that was -- you don't know how he -- I don't know how he got it, is that correct, even though you'd been there for already over a year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes. You have to bear in mind that I did not come when those people were being issued with the weapons. This list contains at least 90 per cent of the men who were no longer members of the unit. The commander ordered us to compile a list of the weapons that had gone missing and that were being looked for and this is the list. For some weapons we knew where they were, we knew where some people were, but not all of them. You can see that very well from the list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is being asked to slow down, otherwise the interpreters cannot vouch for the accuracy of the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, you are again requested to speak slow. Thank you for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you speak about these people in the abstract, but this particular person you actually said you knew. You said he got killed, he left. For a while he was an assistant company commander. Do you deny -- are you telling us that he did not act as a sniper for your company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I'm sure he was not. Ciro Rajko had never served the army. He could not be a sniper. He left and went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at number 39. Do you recognise the person listed under number 39?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: When I joined the unit, that person was not there. He had gone to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Which means that he had taken the weapons that were issued to him at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But this, too, indicates that he took with him a sniper rifle; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Please, I have just told you that he was issued with weapons at the beginning of the war. I don't know what those weapons were. I am just saying that when I was commander and even when Major Loncarevic was commander, we did not have a single sniper rifle in the unit and I'm stating that clear and loud once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go to number 83, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person's name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's the last page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Perhaps I can give the witness a hard copy of this. Oh, I think we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise that name under number 83?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And he too had a sniper rifle; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. That person had left. He had moved out of Bosnia; I don't know where. At the beginning of the war he was a company commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, I'm afraid there are two sets of documents in this number. Could we show page 4 of this document and whether -- check whether it is the same document or different one. In the meantime, Mr. Zurovac, you confirm that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4 in B/C/S. And in English 5 or 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should be the next -- in English it says "Claimed weapons," so could you take up from there, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I think if we could go to page 8 of the English and if there is some -- we can later ensure that this is the correct correlation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On 8 English for 83 we have Blagoje Savic and in the B/C/S we just saw the same name and I said to you: "He too had a sniper rifle, correct?" And you said: "I don't know that person had left, he moved out the of Bosnia; I don't know where. At the beginning of the war he was company commander?" But, sir, my question is: When he left, he left with a sniper rifle. That's what this list represents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You know because you personally know? You personally know he left with a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You have to bear in mind that it often happened that people left weapons -- took weapons, sold it, or when they joined a less dangerous unit -- this was a very risky unit and people defected. Why don't we use the right term.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can look at 89 and we'll just stay with the B/C/S for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 89, above your signature, we have a person named Gusic. Do you see that? And he too has a sniper rifle. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Of course I do. At the beginning of the war, Gusic was seriously wounded and he left and he never reappeared. This is a list of claimed weapons. What the unit had from the beginning of the war and even before sniper squads had been set up with the battalion, I don't know. I don't know how it was set up, whether it was set up at all, if we're talking about a sniper squad. I don't know whether that was set up and how it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us why these people would have left your company with sniper rifles if they themselves were not snipers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Of course I can tell you. I've just told you that people defected. At the beginning of the war those people were probably issued with all those weapons and they took those weapons away. They smuggled. They sold it on the black market. There was black market for everything. Jerko Gusic was probably issued with a rifle. At the beginning of the war he was seriously wounded and he left and went --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear where that person went to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us where that person went to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I believe that he went to Vojvodina. I'm not sure. I did not find him in the unit when I joined it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24077 becomes Exhibit P5991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24076.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a lengthy document. It is actually the log-book for the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I may give a hard copy to the witness and a copy to the Defence because it's otherwise unwieldy to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for the record, I have marked pages in the copy for the witness because those are the pages I'm going to go to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So take a moment, sir, and flip through this and tell me if you recognise this. Sir, do you recognise this particular book or this type of log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No. I don't recognise this, at least I don't recognise the pages that I have leafed through. I did not join the company at that time. I was still imprisoned in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And I see that you're looking at the beginning of the book, but as you go through it, it actually goes into the year 1994 and that was a period of time when you were with the company; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I still haven't reached that part. I'm at the month of July 1992. You say that pages are enumerated. I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you a general question, then. Was it customary for companies to keep a log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did your company keep a log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, why would it keep a log-book, given the fact that there were daily reports. Every day two daily reports were sent. I find this document suspicious. I don't see why a log-book would be kept on top of the two daily reports every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at page 19 in the English and also page 19 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for you, sir, I've put a little green tab on page 19 so you could get to it more readily and I think you're on it now. This is July --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: July 1992. In the right-hand corner it says "4th Platoon" and then "August 1992" on the right-hand side. And then it says Karlo Bauer was issued with a sniper rifle. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to page 34 --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No, no, no, really no -- this is a Croat judging by the first and the last names, so no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 34, please, in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And up in the left-hand corner we see "4th Platoon." It had 400, 7.62-millimetre; 225, 7.9-millimetreS; and 30 for sniper rifle. This appears to be in November 1992 when you came into the company. At that time, were there any sniper rifles in the company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I apologise, how many sniper rifles did you say there were?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm reading what the English says. You can read the B/C/S. It says "30 for sniper rifle." Now, I'm not suggesting that it means 30 sniper rifles. My question to you is: Were there any sniper rifles in the company in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war I don't know. "30 for," do you know what this means? "30 for sniper rifles," not probably even a well-equipped battalion has that, let alone a company with only a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see what unit this is and I can't see anywhere that it says "30 for sniper rifles." And also, what is the provenance of this document? There is no ERN number on what we -- on the document that we see on the screen. We see it in the hard copy but not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I expect to hear that in the coming questions. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to page 45 in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But just while we are on this page in B/C/S, shall we ask the witness to read that fourth line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, if we can go back to page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are on that page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear Judge Kwon's request?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: The 1st Platoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mm-hmm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Platoon -- do you mean the left-hand side of the page or the right-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Left side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Left, which start with "Sare" ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Platoon, I don't have that here. Maybe it is not well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the monitor in front of you? Do you see the fourth line which starts with probably "Sare"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read that line aloud so that we can hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Sare SOK sniper" something, very hard. I don't know what this SOKN means. It's very difficult to read this and discern the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the first line, then, please ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The 1st Platoon - 640 KM," is it, "7.62" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Zurovac, the fourth line should read "Sare 30 KM," doesn't it -- shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Sare 30KM," yes, probably -- I mean I -- this is not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our information is that this document came from the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion of this brigade; however, at this point I will not ask to tender it where the witness himself has not indicated that it was customary in his battalion to keep it. But I'd like to move on to 65 ter 12226, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, sir, you joined the 4th Company in November of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you left sometime in 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When exactly, what month?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I left on the 10th of April or the 10th of March, 1994. I can't remember exactly when, but I went to do work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we're looking at a listing from your company in September of 1993 and it's a listing of wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go -- we can see it both in the English and in the B/C/S. We actually see -- may I have page 5 of the English, please. And the listing in B/C/S is just the same names.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We see your name on this. Were you wounded in September of 1993? And that listing is --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I was. I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And also from the top we see number 3, a Karlo Bauer who was also wounded and this is the same name of the person we just saw in the log-book at page 19 who was issued --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Hold on, please. This is the same name of the person we saw on page 19 in the log-book who was issued a sniper rifle. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No. This name means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 12226 becomes Exhibit P5992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, earlier today at page -- at transcript 57, when we were talking about the siege and I asked you whether you thought the ABiH was justified in breaking the siege and you said: "I suppose it was justified from the point of view of an intention to take the entire state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to place it under control and create a state that would suit the policy of Alija Izetbegovic." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us what his policy was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Establishing an Islamic state of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Separate from that, do you believe that the ethnic groups should not live together under one state and related to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, this doesn't arise out of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond to that or will you move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I was trying to clarify something that he had brought up in the cross, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- what subject do you refer to, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The policy of Alija Izetbegovic, but if Your Honour prefers I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we were just speaking about that policy and you said it was establishing an Islamic state of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. And this is something that you -- a subject matter you spoke of in your statement as well. Now, sir, my question to you is this: During the direct examination Mr. Karadzic briefly asked about your time prior to 1992, and he mentioned that you were in a camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which statement is the Prosecution referring to again? Can we receive this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably in answer to your question. Yes, Ms. West, you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it was -- well, I suppose it would be the final of the four statements of this particular witness. I don't know what the ID number is, but it's the witness's statement. But at this point I was asking about his earlier testimony on direct in which he stated that he was in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you said yes. And was that the Ljubuski camp?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No. I said it was a prison in Mostar, not a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies. But was it at Ljubuski or in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I passed through Ljubuski, not only I but all the prisoners when we were taken away for an exchange in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you just passed through Ljubuski; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Well, there were some beatings behind some sort of a stadium there, then they crammed us into buses, the same ones that they had used to take us there; and we were taken for an exchange at Todorovic's near Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier statement - and this can be of any one of them - it's paragraph 9, you said: "I was transferred from Mostar to Ljubuski and I suffered even greater misery and beatings there. When they arrested me I weighed 99 kilos" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, this is beyond the scope of direct and particularly unfair given the fact that the Chamber said that this material was irrelevant so we didn't lead it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During the direct he spoke about his time at the camp, and although we did have a discussion about the material being irrelevant, in paragraph 11 of his statement he indicates that -- he speaks about his motivation for joining the SRK, which is related to this camp and that's why I'm getting into it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he say "camp"?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have more to conclude your cross-examination, Ms. West? How much more do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to qualify what Ljubuski was, but as a result of being there you indicated that you sobered up in paragraph 11 of your statement. You said that: "... increasing obvious hatred that the Croats and Muslims had toward the Serbs forced us to sober up and see the falseness of brotherhood and unity and to think back to the suffering of the Serbs in the First and Second World Wars, when we were exterminated en masse." Can you tell us what you mean by "sober up"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Of course. In the Second World War I was left without my parents. The Serbs have a historical memory such as it is and to avoid 1941 from being repeated when the Serbs in Herzegovina were killed en masse, when pits in Herzegovina were filled with Serbian corpses, in order to make sure that this didn't happen to me and to all Serbs, well, 150.000 Serbs fled from Sarajevo in order to avoid such things happening to them, things that happened to them in the First World War and the Second World War. This shows that they sobered up. They sobered up in the sense that people came to their senses. Were they to wait for them to be thrown into a pit again, into the same pit that my father was thrown into, was I to be thrown into such a pit? To prevent such things from happening, it's quite natural that I behaved as I did and everyone else had no choice. They were faced with a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two or three questions, Your Excellency, very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zurovac, when we spoke about indiscriminate fire on positions, what was hit in that indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: On the whole we knew where their positions were, where our positions were, and so on. They would destroy buildings, private houses, in indiscriminate firing so there was nowhere for us to sleep, nowhere for us to take shelter. They would destroy houses, anything that might serve a man was, quite simply, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many private houses were destroyed in this indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Everything on our combat line a hundred per cent. There are documents, there's footage after Dayton, and everything shows that all those houses were destroyed. Unfortunately, they are still in that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a new translation in which the term "randomly" would be changed to "indiscriminately." Nonselective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was there any firing in the depth?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilian casualties and was that as a result of fire snipers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: On the whole as a result of sniper fire, to a certain extent as a result of artillery fire, but most of the casualties sustained were sustained as a result of sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked about who had snipers, you asked about what a Tandzara is. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: A Tandzara is an M48 rifle, an old Yugoslav rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of whether there were any sights available, did you have snipers to whom you as a commander assigned tasks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask you about the theoretical implications of a siege. What was the combat task that your company had?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Defence exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: Houses, territory, ancestral land, the places where we were born, where we lived. This was a working area and the population was 90 per cent Serbs, so we were defending our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zurovac.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN ZUROVAC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards your request for retranslation, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber will leave it at that. Simply, if you need to -- if you like that part retranslated, I would like you to put it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zurovac, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't know if the Chamber was about to rise or wanted to raise another matter, but there's one quick matter I think I need to address before we adjourn. So you just let me know when you think the time is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you have the floor, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I simply wanted to respond to an e-mail that Mr. Robinson sent concerning a proposed change in the witness order and I'm afraid we do have to protest against this effort for the following reason. As the Defence and I believe the Trial Chamber are both aware, we are required by necessity to prioritise the translation and therefore the subsequent analysis of documents potentially to be used in cross-examination. And in that connection, the multiple shifts in the witness order that have already taken place in the past week or so have strained those resources and, therefore, the ability and the capacity of the responsible attorney to deal with the material that is capable of shedding light on the events at issue and potentially the credibility of the witness. So on the heels of those previous changes, this does unfairly disadvantage us, and I raise that point. Now, I want to be clear, I'm not asserting that it is impossible and, as always, we're prepared to do our utmost to accommodate the Chamber. But particularly given the fact that this appears to be some theoretical concern about the return of the witness which we believe could be adequately addressed simply by commencing the witness's examination-in-chief and having the witness then return, as we would presumably do by retaining the current order, we consider that the impact on the Prosecution under these circumstances would be unduly unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear, next one is Malinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in any event, the witness in question was one of the witnesses we were supposed to conclude by the end of this week -- this week, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not originally, but as things ultimately transpired, yes. But as I say, that -- that, as I recollect, is a result of multiple changes that ultimately accelerated that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted that you commented you would be able to deal with it, but after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- court session I would like you to have a word with the Defence team and sort it out in a -- in a more co-operative way. Whether it's -- please discuss it with the Defence and then come back to the Chamber tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before we adjourn, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber would like to hear from you tomorrow morning on the following subject. The Chamber has stated on a number of occasions that although it will not impose time-limits on the Prosecution's cross-examination just yet, it would continue to closely monitor the conduct of trial. Having heard 21 witnesses excluding the current -- the last witness, Dusan Zurovac, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution has used much more time on cross-examination than the accused on both examination-in-chief and re-examination. The Chamber also notes that for the overwhelming majority of these witnesses the evidence presented pursuant to Rule 92 ter was extremely limited with short statements and very few associated exhibits, if any. Often, the witnesses' Rule 92 ter evidence also focuses on a limited number of issues. The Chamber would, therefore, like to hear from you tomorrow for first thing on the issue of time spent by the Prosecution on cross-examination. The hearing is now adjourned. We will sit here at Courtroom 3 at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
